ideas.title: Crystal Cavern
ideas.concept: Players compete to claim a shared hex-tiled cave floor by stacking translucent crystal shards on pegs, with taller stacks worth contested territory but at real risk of toppling. A turn feels like deciding whether to reach for a big central hex with a risky third crystal, or play it safe on the edges while your rivals gamble.
ideas.differentiation: Base concept: Reef (Next Move Games) — personal-board stacking of reef pieces scored by top-down pattern matching, no dexterity element, no direct player interaction on the board. Specific rule changes here: (1) all players build on ONE shared central board instead of personal boards, so placements directly contest territory; (2) stacks are physically peg-mounted and can topple, adding a real dexterity/push-your-luck risk absent from Reef; (3) scoring is area-majority by hex ownership (tallest stack color) rather than pattern-matching a personal board from above. Confirmed via search ('stacking vertical reef building tile game area majority') that Reef is the closest existing product and is a calm, no-dexterity personal-board euro — the shared-board-plus-toppling-risk combination was not found in any shipped product in that search.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 10+. Setup: assemble a 19-hex modular cave-floor board (fewer hexes for 2-3 players), each hex printed with a peg and a point value 1-3. Each player takes 15 crystal pieces (5 small/5 medium/5 large) in their color and 3 Fracture tokens. On your turn, take ONE action: (a) place one crystal from your supply onto any empty hex peg, or stack it on an existing crystal (small crystals may only rest atop medium/large, never the reverse) — the hex is 'owned' by whoever has the tallest crystal in that stack; or (b) draw one Tremor chip from the draw box, naming a hex zone — lightly tap the board once; any stack in that zone that visibly wobbles or falls is removed from play (lost, not returned). Once per game, spend a Fracture token to remove the top crystal from any stack into your own supply; if this changes hex ownership you gain a 1 VP steal marker. Game ends when all crystals are placed or lost, or any player empties their supply of 15; finish the round. Scoring: sum the printed values of hexes you own (tie = no one scores) plus steal markers; highest total wins, ties broken by fewest crystals lost.
ideas.components: 19 interlocking hex floor tiles (PLA, ~4cm across, 3mm thick, raised locking nub + 5mm peg, embossed point value 1-3, 4 with a tilted 'Uneven' peg variant); 60 crystal pieces (15 per player x4 colors, 3 sizes 15-35mm tall, translucent PLA/resin, peg-hole base for 3-tier stacking); 12 engraved Tremor chips (25mm PLA discs, printed zone diagram); 12 Fracture tokens (15mm gear-shaped chips, 3 per player); 4 VP steal markers (12mm star chips); 1 printed lidded draw box (8x8x5cm, slide lid) for random Tremor draws; 1 printed lidded storage box (~22x22x8cm) with tile-nesting insert.
ideas.demand_case: Dexterity board games are a large proven BGG category (1,000+ published titles) and area-control tile-drafting games (the Azul/Reef family) have sold well over a million combined units, showing strong crossover demand for exactly this drafting-plus-stacking family. Target audience: family and light-hobbyist game night, ages 10+, existing Reef/Azul owners looking for a more physically tense follow-up.
ideas.fun_case: Every turn poses the same 'reach for the valuable center hex vs. play safe on the edge' tension that has kept Reef and Azul commercially strong, sharpened by the real physical stakes of a wobble-check absent from either — the same 'just one more piece' thrill validated by Bausack and Tetra Tower's dexterity sales. 30-45 minute playtime fits the stated family/hobbyist audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 19 hex tiles and 3 crystal-size geometries (x4 colors) is an efficient, low-unique-file print run. The peg/hole joint repeats up to 15 times per player (60 total) — the compounding-risk case: mitigated by a generous 5mm tapered peg and a hard 3-crystal stack cap, so no chain exceeds 2 joints deep despite the high piece count. Tremor/Fracture/VP chips are simple flat engraved discs, low risk. The draw box's slide lid is the one moving-part component; keep the channel tolerance at 0.5mm+ to avoid binding.

Beside the board sit small engraved wooden-look tremor chips, tiny gear-shaped fracture tokens, and a small printed storage box with a sliding lid, all arranged on a dark wood table, overhead angled product-photography lighting, warm dramatic shadows.

ideas.title: Gearform
ideas.concept: A tile-drafting game in the Azul family, but the tiles are real interlocking gears — you can only place a drafted gear where it will physically mesh with its neighbor, proven by spinning it in place. Every turn is the familiar 'which color do I take or deny' drafting choice plus a live spatial-fit puzzle to actually seat the piece.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Azul (drafting colored tiles from shared racks into a personal grid, scored by completed patterns). Specific rule change: drafted tiles are gear-shaped with real printed teeth; a tile may only be placed adjacent to an already-placed gear if their tooth counts share a common factor greater than 1, verified physically by rotating the two gears together — a mismatch visibly collides rather than spins freely. This mechanical-fit legality check, plus locking-pin-based chain scoring, replaces Azul's purely visual pattern-line scoring. Searched 'gear meshing tile drafting board game mechanic' and 'gear tile puzzle board game interlocking teeth alignment' — found IQ Gears (a solitaire spatial logic puzzle with no drafting, opponents, or scoring track) as the closest gear-mesh product, confirming no existing drafting game uses a physical gear-mesh legality check.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 10+. Setup: fill Foundry racks (5/7/9 racks by player count) with 4 random gear tiles each from the shared draw box; each player takes a 5x5-hub personal Workshop board. On your turn, draft ALL gear tiles of one color from one rack (or the shared overflow pool), then place every drafted tile one at a time onto your Workshop: a tile may only be seated on a hub adjacent to an already-placed gear if their tooth counts share a common factor greater than 1 (checked by physically trying to spin the pair together); any drafted tile that cannot legally be placed goes to your Scrap tray. Any straight-line chain of 3+ same-color meshed gears scores immediately (2 VP per gear) and is locked with a pin, remaining on the board as a future adjacency reference. Refill racks and repeat for 6 rounds. Scoring: total locked-chain VP, minus 1 VP per Scrap tile, plus 3 VP if your Workshop ends completely full; highest total wins, ties broken by fewest Scrap tiles.
ideas.components: 100 gear tiles (20 unique STL files: 5 colors x 4 tooth-count variants x5 copies each, ~3cm diameter PLA discs with printed teeth and a snap-peg underside that still allows free spin); 4 personal Workshop boards (5x5 raised-hub grids, ~18x18cm PLA); 9 Foundry rack trays (each holding 4 tiles upright, ~10x3cm PLA); 20 locking pins (8mm grey PLA pegs); 4 Scrap trays (6x6cm shallow dishes); 1 printed lidded draw box for random rack refills; 1 printed lidded storage case sized to nest all boards and tiles.
ideas.demand_case: Azul won the 2017 Spiel des Jahres and has sold over a million copies across its line (Azul, Summer Pavilion, Sagrada, Calico all extend the drafting-into-personal-grid genre), showing a large, proven family/hobbyist audience for this exact turn structure. Target audience: family and light-hobbyist gamers who already own an Azul-like and want a fresh puzzle layer within the familiar frame.
ideas.fun_case: Each turn keeps Azul's proven 'which color to take or deny' tension while adding a genuine spatial-fit sub-puzzle, echoing the appeal of the mechanical-puzzle market (IQ Gears, Archimedes' Gear) layered onto a scoring structure already validated by Azul's commercial success. 30-45 minute playtime matches the audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 100 tiles reduce to 20 unique STL files, an efficient batch. The snap-peg-into-hub joint repeats 25 times per board (100 across 4 boards) — the flagged compounding-joint risk — mitigated by specifying a loose spin-fit (6mm peg, 6.4mm bore) rather than a tight snap, since a loose fit still demonstrates mesh/no-mesh via tooth collision and avoids tolerance drift causing binding across a large print run. Gear teeth are sized at a 3mm minimum pitch for FDM reliability, no feature under 1mm. Locking pins use a single friction-fit hole per gear, low risk.

ideas.title: Driftwood Dice Forge
ideas.concept: A push-your-luck dice game where a real spiral ramp tower decides where three dice land, but before you drop them, every player secretly dials in a prediction of the outcome. Each turn mixes the physical thrill of watching dice spiral down with the tension of a blind, simultaneous bet everyone at the table has a stake in.
ideas.differentiation: This is an original synthesis of push-your-luck dice mechanics with a physical ramp component and a simultaneous secret-prediction layer, not a rule-change of one specific named title. Searched 'dice ramp push your luck prediction bidding pocket board game' — found no existing shipped game combining a physical multi-pocket ramp outcome with a simultaneous prediction-dial mechanic (results returned only standard push-your-luck games like Can't Stop, Zombie Dice, and Tally Up!, none of which use a physical outcome ramp or a prediction layer).
ideas.rules: 2-5 players, ages 8+. Setup: place the Forge Ramp (a 6-pocket spiral chute, pockets valued 1-6) in the center; each player takes a Prediction Dial and 8 Ingot tokens as a starting bank. On the active Smith's turn, ALL players (including the Smith) secretly set their Prediction Dial to the pocket number they think will be the majority result, then reveal simultaneously. The Smith drops the 3 shared Forge Dice one at a time into the ramp; whichever pocket number appears on the most dice (ties won by highest number) is the Result. Any player whose dial matched the Result earns Ingots equal to that pocket's value. The Smith may then bank their own earnings or push their luck: re-drop only the dice that did NOT match the Result — if this changes the Result and the Smith's own prediction no longer matches, the Smith loses ALL Ingots earned that turn. Turn passes clockwise; the game ends after every player has been Smith 4 times. Most Ingots banked wins, ties broken by fewest failed pushes.
ideas.components: 1 Forge Ramp tower (spiral chute, ~20cm tall x12cm base, PLA/PETG, printed in 3 pegged sections: funnel, spiral body, 6-pocket rosette base); 3 Forge Dice (25mm PLA/resin cubes, engraved forge-hammer pips 1-6); 5 Prediction Dials (6cm PLA discs with a snap-fit rotating pointer arm); 60 Ingot tokens (12 per player, 15mm bronze-look hexagonal chips, embossed value); 1 printed lidded storage box (~25x20x22cm) sized to nest the ramp sections and tokens.
ideas.demand_case: Push-your-luck dice games are one of the largest-selling family categories (Can't Stop, Zombie Dice, and King of Tokyo each carry tens of thousands of BGG ratings), and dice-tower/ramp components are independently documented as a strong standalone seller in the 3D-printed tabletop hobby market. Target audience: family game night and casual dice-game fans, ages 8+.
ideas.fun_case: The bank-vs-push decision is the same durable tension behind Can't Stop's 40+ year track record, intensified here because every player has a stake in every turn via the simultaneous prediction (no one is idle waiting their turn), plus the genuine tactile satisfaction of watching physical dice spiral down a real ramp. 20-30 minute playtime suits the stated audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: The ramp is the highest-risk component: its spiral interior must be split into printable sub-sections (funnel/spiral/base) joined by generous peg-and-socket seams (4mm peg, 0.3mm clearance) rather than printed as one monolithic spiral, and the die-drop channel needs at least 4mm of clearance beyond the die's diagonal to avoid FDM-surface jams — flagged as the riskiest tolerance in this idea and worth physical prototyping before a full production run. Prediction dials use one rotating friction-fit joint each (5 total, low risk at that count). All other components are simple flat or embossed chips.

ideas.title: Depth Chase
ideas.concept: A hidden-movement pursuit game where a lone Smuggler evades Patrol boats across a harbor board that gets rebuilt from modular tiles every game, tracked only by a rotating zone dial instead of a pencil-and-pad log. A turn feels like narrowing down a fog of possible hiding spots that never plays the same way twice.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Scotland Yard (asymmetric hidden-movement pursuit, one evader vs. several seekers, tracked via a written movement log on a fixed printed map). Specific rule changes: (1) the harbor board is assembled from 12 reconfigurable modular tiles, so the map differs every session instead of Scotland Yard's single fixed map; (2) position tracking uses a physical rotating zone dial revealing only a coarse color-zone, not an exact-move log, replacing pencil-and-pad tracking with a mechanical component; (3) a shared limited-use Sonar Ping token gives a binary near/far check in place of Scotland Yard's fixed reveal-turn structure. Searched 'hidden movement board game modular board sonar dial tracker' — the closest real-time match, Captain Sonar, is a simultaneous team-communication game with no hidden evading player and no modular board, confirming this specific modular-board-plus-mechanical-dial combination for a Scotland Yard-style pursuit is not an existing shipped product.
ideas.rules: 3-5 players (1 Smuggler, 2-4 Patrol), ages 10+. Setup: players jointly arrange the 12 hex harbor tiles into any agreed layout (different every game), place the Smuggler Sub under the opaque dome, and set 4 Patrol Boats on fixed docks; the Smuggler's Fuel Track starts at 12. Each round: Smuggler Phase — the Smuggler secretly moves 1-3 spaces along printed channels under the dome, spending 1 fuel per tile; every 3rd round is a Surface round, where the Smuggler must set the Position Dial to their current color zone (a broad multi-tile region, never an exact tile). Patrol Phase — each Patrol Boat moves up to 4 spaces; Patrol may spend one of 3 shared Sonar Ping tokens per game to get a yes/no check on whether the Smuggler is within 2 tiles. Patrol wins immediately if any boat ends its move on the Smuggler's exact hidden tile. Smuggler wins by surviving 12 rounds or reaching one of 3 Open Sea exit tiles; if Fuel reaches 0, the Smuggler must reveal their exact position every round from then on.
ideas.components: 12 modular harbor hex-tiles (~10cm across, PLA, double-sided printed channel/dock patterns and 6 color zones, keyed interlocking edges with a 4mm tongue and 0.4mm clearance); 1 Smuggler Sub miniature (3cm PLA); 4 Patrol Boat miniatures (3cm PLA, 4 colors); 1 opaque dome token (5cm hollow hemisphere, opaque black PLA); 1 Position Dial (8cm disc with 6 printed color zones and a snap-fit rotating pointer); 1 Fuel Track strip (12-pip indent track with a sliding peg marker); 3 anchor-shaped Sonar Ping tokens (15mm); 1 printed lidded storage box (~22x22x6cm) with tile-nesting insert.
ideas.demand_case: Hidden-movement pursuit is an established BGG mechanic category with durable demand — Scotland Yard alone carries 20,000+ BGG ratings and has stayed in continuous print since 1983, with Fury of Dracula and Letters from Whitechapel extending the audience. Target audience: family/hobbyist crossover groups, ages 10+, who enjoy deduction-and-chase games and want replayability beyond a fixed map.
ideas.fun_case: Patrol's core loop is the same deductive narrowing that has kept Scotland Yard in print for over 40 years, while the Smuggler's turn is a real routing/bluffing puzzle over which channel avoids giving away too much on a Surface round. The modular board directly answers the single most common critique of the fixed-map original: repeat-play staleness. 45-60 minute playtime suits the stated audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: 12 double-sided tiles produce 24 unique face designs from one reusable hex-tile geometry (texture-only variation), an efficient print. The keyed interlocking edge is reassembled repeatedly across many games, so it uses a looser locating-nub friction edge (4mm tongue, 0.4mm clearance) rather than a tight snap-fit, avoiding wear/cracking from repeated reconfiguration — this is the compounding-risk feature (12 tiles x multiple reassemblies) and is explicitly de-risked by loosening rather than tightening tolerance. The dome's interior rim needs no undercut sharper than 45 degrees so it lifts cleanly without dragging the hidden piece. The Position Dial's single rotating joint is low risk.

ideas.title: Aqueduct Alley
ideas.concept: A path-laying race where channel tiles stack across two physical elevation levels so routes can cross over and under each other, and instead of sliding an abstract token you watch a real marble roll through the maze you built. Every placement is a bet on whether your channel reaches your cistern first or gets undercut by a rival's ramp.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Tsuro (flat single-level path-tile laying, tokens slide along completed paths, no elevation). Specific rule change: tiles exist on two physical levels (Ground and Elevated) connected by dedicated Ramp tiles, letting routes physically cross over/under each other — a spatial dimension Tsuro's flat board cannot represent — and tokens are replaced by real marbles that mechanically roll along carved grooves rather than being manually slid. Searched 'Tsuro variant elevated bridge crossing tiles two-level path game' — results covered known fan variants (Crossing Paths, Longest Path, 2-player double-token) but none involving a physical two-level elevation system, confirming this specific combination is not an existing product.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 8+. Setup: assemble the 4x4 base grid platform with raised corner posts; each player places a marble at a random edge Source tile and a Cistern collector at their chosen home edge. Each player draws a personal rack of 3 Channel Tiles from the shared supply of 36. On your turn, place one tile from your rack onto any open grid position at Ground or Elevated level (Ramp tiles must be placed where a ground slot and elevated slot stack at the same position); any marble whose channel now connects rolls automatically along the groove until it hits a dead end, a fork (owner chooses direction next time it's reached), or the board edge (that marble is eliminated). Draw back up to 3 tiles. First player to roll their marble into their own Cistern funnel wins outright; if the tile supply runs out first, whoever's marble traveled through the most tiles (tracked on a simple counter) wins.
ideas.components: 1 base grid platform (16x16cm PLA, 16 raised 2cm corner posts); 36 Channel Tiles (4x4cm x4mm PLA squares, engraved grooves 6.5mm wide x4mm deep sized for a 10mm marble, printed with level designation); 12 Elevated-tier clip tiles (blank support tiles that clip onto posts to form the second level, same 4x4cm footprint); 4 marbles (10mm glass or resin, one per player color); 4 Cistern collection funnels (clip-on cup pieces, one per player color); 4 personal tile racks (small printed stands holding 3 tiles upright); 1 printed lidded storage box (~20x20x8cm).
ideas.demand_case: Tsuro is a well-established family path-laying game still in active retail print (Calliope Games) with 10,000+ BGG ratings, showing strong sustained demand for simple tile-laying games with instant tactile feedback. Target audience: family game night, ages 8+, including younger kids drawn to the physical marble-rolling feedback.
ideas.fun_case: Every placement carries Tsuro's proven 'route yourself to safety, route rivals to doom' tension, intensified by the elevation dimension (a tile that looks safe on one level can be undercut by a later ramp) and made more viscerally satisfying by watching a real marble physically complete your construction rather than sliding an abstract token — validated by both Tsuro's commercial longevity and the broad appeal of marble-run toys. 20-30 minute playtime matches the audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: Groove tolerance is the main risk: grooves are specified 0.5mm oversized (6.5mm for a 10mm marble) and should be test-fit before a full batch of 48 tiles to avoid binding on FDM layer lines. The post/clip joint for the elevated tier repeats across 16 posts and up to 12 elevated tiles — mitigated by using a simple vertical friction peg rather than a cantilevered snap-hook, since repeated assembly/disassembly across many games would otherwise fatigue a hook feature. All tiles are flat engraved geometry with no feature under 1mm once groove width is fixed.

ideas.title: Embercraft
ideas.concept: A trick-taking game where nobody plays in turn order — every player secretly slots a tile into a shared rotating kiln, and all tiles flip open at once. A turn feels less like reading the table and more like guessing what everyone else is blindly about to commit, right up until the reveal.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: classic trick-taking (Hearts, Bridge, Spades, The Crew) — plays are made sequentially, so later players see earlier plays before choosing. Specific rule change: all players place their tile face-down into their own numbered Kiln slot simultaneously, then every slot is revealed together — removing the sequential information entirely and replacing it with blind, simultaneous commitment. Searched 'simultaneous reveal trick-taking card game no turn order' — found trick-taking games with simultaneous secret-role selection or simultaneous bidding rounds, but no example of a fully sequential-play trick-taking game converted to fully simultaneous per-trick reveal, confirming this specific structural change is not an existing shipped product.
ideas.rules: 3-5 players, ages 10+. Setup: shuffle the 36 Ember Tiles (4 suits red/blue/green/white, ranks 1-9) and deal evenly into personal racks (9 each for 4 players; adjust with a dummy tray for 3 or 5). Each trick: all players simultaneously choose one tile from their rack and place it face-down into their own slot on the central Kiln board, then all slots are opened together. The tile of the suit matching the trick's Draft suit (marked by a fixed pointer on the Kiln's rim) with the highest rank wins the trick; if no one played the Draft suit, the highest tile overall wins. The winner takes all played tiles as their trick pile (1 VP each at game end), and their highest-ranked suit played becomes the next trick's Draft suit. Continue until racks are empty (9 tricks for 4 players). Scoring: 1 VP per tile in your trick pile, plus a 3 VP bonus for whoever won the most tricks using their own suit's rank-1 tile (a sacrifice bonus); highest total wins.
ideas.components: 36 Ember Tiles (3x3cm PLA engraved square chips, 4 suit colors, embossed numerals 1-9, translucent 'flame' resin cast); 1 Kiln board (20cm rotating PLA disc with 5 radial covered slide-lid slots and a fixed Draft-suit pointer on the rim); 5 personal tile racks (small stands holding up to 9 tiles upright); 5 trick-pile trays (shallow dishes for won tricks); 1 printed lidded storage box (~22x22x8cm).
ideas.demand_case: Trick-taking is one of the largest and most durable game categories worldwide (Hearts, Spades, Bridge, and Euchre represent one of tabletop gaming's largest player bases; modern hobby trick-taker The Crew alone carries 30,000+ BGG ratings), showing enormous built-in demand for the core mechanic. Target audience: hobbyist card-game players and family groups who already play trick-taking games and want a physical, non-paper variant.
ideas.fun_case: The core decision shifts from 'what does the board tell me to play' to 'what will everyone else blindly commit,' a genuinely different cognitive task validated by the strength of blind-commitment mechanics in games like Skull and For Sale, layered onto trick-taking's proven suit-following/scoring skeleton. 30-40 minute playtime suits a card-game-night group.
ideas.producibility_notes: The Kiln board's 5 slide-lid slots are the highest-risk repeated feature; a slide-channel lid (rather than a pin hinge) tolerates FDM layer-line friction better at this scale, and one slot's fit should be validated before duplicating to all 5. Tile engraving (numeral + suit icon) must stay at or above 1.2mm line width/depth to remain legible on a single-color print. No other component carries elevated joint risk.

ideas.title: Meridian Peaks
ideas.concept: Chinese Checkers stretched across three stacked star-shaped tiers connected by ramps, so a jump chain can now go up or down as well as sideways. Every turn is the familiar hop-over-a-piece decision, but now with a vertical dimension that reshapes which jumps are even possible.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Chinese Checkers (single flat star board, pieces move by single steps or chained jumps to reach the opposite home point). Specific rule change: the board is split into 3 stacked star tiers of decreasing size connected at 6 fixed Ramp points, where a piece can traverse between tiers as part of a normal move or as a jump-chain segment, and the win condition requires relocating all pieces to a home point on a DIFFERENT tier (Summit) than the starting tier (Ground), forcing mandatory use of the new vertical dimension. Searched 'Chinese checkers multi-level 3D elevated board game' — found only flat single-level 3D-printable Chinese Checkers files (e.g. on Cults3D) and standard commercial editions, confirming no existing shipped product uses a multi-tier ramp-connected board.
ideas.rules: 2, 3, or 6 players, ages 8+. Setup: assemble the 3 stacked star tiers (Ground 30cm, Mid 24cm, Summit 18cm) on their support columns, each tier a standard 121-hole star pattern; each player's 10 marbles start in their home point on the Ground tier. On your turn, move one marble either by a single step to an adjacent empty hole, or by a chain of jumps over adjacent occupied holes into empty holes beyond (standard Chinese Checkers rules) within a tier; additionally, if your piece occupies a Ramp hole and the aligned hole on the neighboring tier is empty, you may move it up or down the ramp as a normal step or as one segment of a multi-jump chain. The goal is to move all 10 of your marbles into your designated home point on the SUMMIT tier (not your starting tier). First player to relocate all 10 marbles to their Summit home wins.
ideas.components: 3 nested star tier boards (PLA, 30cm/24cm/18cm point-to-point, each with 121 shallow 10.5mm holes, mounted on removable support-leg columns at fixed 6cm vertical spacing, each leg secured by a single locating pin rather than a press-fit); 6 ramp connector pieces (short chutes bridging aligned Ramp holes between tiers); 60 marbles (10mm, 6 colors, 10 per player); 1 printed lidded storage box (~32x32x20cm) for the knock-down (legs removable) stack.
ideas.demand_case: Chinese Checkers is one of the best-known abstract strategy games globally, in continuous commercial production since the 1890s under various names with dozens of active retail editions (e.g. WE Games) and an estimated player base in the tens of millions. Target audience: family and casual abstract-strategy players, ages 8+, who already know Chinese Checkers and want a novel physical variant.
ideas.fun_case: The core jump-chain-planning decision is unchanged and proven over more than a century of continuous play, but the mandatory vertical dimension forces genuinely new spatial planning across 3 stacked patterns instead of one flat one — the same 'familiar rules, new dimension' appeal that has made added-dimension twists on classic abstracts (3D tic-tac-toe and similar) a recurring successful format. 20-40 minute playtime matches the audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: This is the most parts-heavy idea in the set (3 boards, 6 columns, 6 ramps, 60 marbles). The riskiest feature is vertical alignment across 3 tiers at the 6 ramp points: holes are toleranced at 10.5mm for a 10mm marble, and each support leg uses a single locating pin rather than a friction press-fit specifically because repeated tier removal for storage would wear out a tight fit. The design explicitly ships knock-down (legs unclip) both to reduce shipping volume and to prevent the vertical-alignment joint from fatiguing across repeated setup/teardown.

ideas.title: Cairn Climbers
ideas.concept: Every player builds their own stone cairn, but all the cairns stand on one shared tilting plate, so a rival's risky placement can topple your tower too. A turn is a blind draw of an oddly-shaped stone and a decision: add it now and share the risk you're creating for everyone, or bank your height and step back.
ideas.differentiation: Base mechanic: shared-tower dexterity stacking (Bausack, Tetra Tower, Shakewave) — in all of these, players stack pieces onto ONE shared tower/platform. Specific rule change: each player builds their OWN separate cairn within a marked zone, but all cairns stand on a single shared Wobble Plate, so any player's placement can destabilize every cairn simultaneously, and individual towers (not one shared tower) are scored by height. Searched 'shared tilting platform multiple personal towers stacking dexterity board game' — found Tetra Tower, Tower Stack, and Shakewave, all of which use one shared tower/stack rather than multiple simultaneous personal towers on a common unstable base, confirming this specific multi-tower structure is not an existing shipped product.
ideas.rules: 2-4 players, ages 8+. Setup: place the Wobble Plate (a platform balanced on a rounded central pivot foot) in the center, with 4 marked Zone circles near its rim; fill the draw box with 30 irregular Stone pieces. On your turn, draw the next unseen Stone from the box (revealing it now for the first time) and place it on top of your OWN cairn within your Zone (never a rival's), then tap the table edge once as a standardized settle check — if the Wobble Plate tips past its printed tilt-limit groove, or any piece on any cairn falls, you must remove your own top 2 stones as Lost (-1 VP each; a cairn that falls to zero scores 0 regardless). Instead of drawing, you may voluntarily bank on your turn, locking your current height as final. The game ends when the stone box is empty or only one player has not yet banked (they finish their turn, then the game ends). Scoring: your cairn's stone count minus Lost penalties; highest total wins.
ideas.components: 1 Wobble Plate assembly (22cm PLA/PETG platform on a 6cm hemispherical pivot base, 2-part printed, with 4 printed Zone outlines and a tilt-limit groove ring); 30 Stone pieces (irregular low-poly rock shapes, 2-5cm, single grey stone-texture PLA, 10 unique STL shapes at 3 scale tiers); 1 printed lidded draw box for blind stone draws; 4 Lost-stone trays (8x8cm dishes, one per player); 1 printed lidded storage box (~26x26x14cm).
ideas.demand_case: Dexterity/stacking games are a proven, large family category (Jenga alone has sold 80M+ units worldwide, and the BGG dexterity mechanic category lists 1,000+ published titles), with shared-instability multiplayer stacking specifically (Bausack, Tetra Tower) showing sustained demand within that space. Target audience: family game night and party-game groups, ages 8+.
ideas.fun_case: The draw-then-decide tension is the same 'just one more' push-your-luck thrill that has kept Jenga and Bausack perennial sellers, sharpened here by direct multiplayer interaction — everyone shares the destabilizing risk even though towers are individually owned, a structural difference from the single-shared-tower format of Tetra Tower and Bausack. 20-30 minute playtime suits the audience.
ideas.producibility_notes: The pivot-foot/Wobble Plate joint is the single highest-risk feature in this idea — though it appears only once (not repeated), it must be tuned so the plate tips predictably rather than randomly; a starting 3cm dome radius is specified but should be physically prototyped and iterated before the STL is locked, flagged here as the riskiest tolerance in the set. Stone pieces carry no joints and are low risk despite high count. Draw box and trays are simple flat/shell prints.

ideas.title: Asteroid Belt Mancala
ideas.concept: The classic Kalah mancala ruleset restyled as an asteroid-mining outpost, with hexagonal crater pods standing in for pits and faceted metallic ore nuggets standing in for seeds. A turn is the same satisfying sow-and-capture loop mancala players already know, just dressed as a deep-space mining run.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Mancala (standard Kalah ruleset), with no rule changes. Styling concept: an asteroid-mining theme — hexagonal 'asteroid pods' replace round pits, a rust/charcoal asteroid-surface board texture replaces plain wood, and faceted metallic 'ore nugget' tokens replace seeds, with two purely cosmetic ore tones (no rule effect). Searched 'honeycomb mancala 3d print bee theme board game' and 'asteroid mining mancala space theme 3d print board game' — found an existing shipped 'Beehive Mancala' (honeycomb/bee/pollen theme) which is why that theme was avoided, and found no existing mancala reskin using an asteroid-mining theme; the closest results were unrelated asteroid-mining worker-placement games (Periorbis, Darkrock Ventures), confirming this specific theme-on-mancala pairing is unclaimed.
ideas.rules: 2 players, ages 6+. Standard Kalah rules, unchanged: the board has 2 rows of 6 pods plus 2 larger end Stations (one per player). Setup: place 4 ore tokens in each of the 12 small pods; Stations start empty. On your turn, pick up all tokens from any one of your own pods and sow them one at a time counterclockwise into each following pod/Station, skipping the opponent's Station. If your last token lands in your own Station, take another turn. If your last token lands in an empty pod on your own side, capture that token plus all tokens in the directly opposite opponent pod into your Station. The game ends when one side's 6 pods are all empty; the other player sweeps their remaining tokens into their own Station. Highest token total in your Station wins.
ideas.components: 1 board (2x6 hexagonal asteroid pods plus 2 larger crater-shaped end Stations, ~40x16cm PLA, asteroid-surface texture, dark grey/rust color, pods sized 18mm diameter x12mm depth minimum); 48 ore tokens (12mm faceted nugget shapes, metallic-look PLA/resin, 2 cosmetic tones silver/gold, both worth 1 point with no rule impact); 1 printed lidded storage box (~42x18x6cm) shaped to nest the board.
ideas.demand_case: Mancala is one of the oldest and most widely played game families globally, with dozens of modern commercial editions in continuous retail (multiple SKUs on Amazon/Target carrying thousands of combined ratings), and asteroid-mining is a currently active indie board game theme (multiple recently Kickstarter-funded titles like Darkrock Ventures and Periorbis show real buyer interest in the theme). Target audience: family game night, ages 6+, general mancala buyers seeking a fresh visual take.
ideas.fun_case: The underlying Kalah ruleset is a proven, centuries-tested 'simple rules, real depth' abstract strategy game already validated by mancala's enormous historical install base; this reskin's role is purely to make that proven gameplay visually fresh for a sci-fi-leaning buyer who might not otherwise choose a plain wooden mancala set, the same audience-expansion logic behind most successful themed toy-aisle reskins.
ideas.producibility_notes: Simplest producibility profile in the set: 1 board plus 1 token geometry (2 cosmetic color variants) plus a box, with no moving joints, snap-fits, or assembly required. Pod depth is specified at 18mm diameter x12mm depth minimum to comfortably hold 15+ tokens late-game without overflow. No feature under 1mm.

ideas.title: Orbital Mill
ideas.concept: Nine Men's Morris redrawn as a solar system, with three concentric orbital rings replacing the traditional nested squares and small planet-shaped tokens standing in for pieces. A turn is the same mill-forming, opponent-blocking classic abstract, just staged among orbiting worlds.
ideas.differentiation: Base game: Nine Men's Morris, with no rule changes. Styling concept: the traditional 3-nested-square board is redrawn as 3 concentric circular orbital rings with radial 'gravity lane' connectors (preserving the identical point/line topology), on a navy star-field board, with small spherical planet/moon-shaped tokens in two colors replacing flat discs. Searched 'solar system nine men's morris planetary board game' — found only standard commercial Nine Men's Morris editions (WE Games, NewVenture Games) and no existing solar-system-themed variant, confirming this specific theme pairing is unclaimed.
ideas.rules: 2 players, ages 8+. Standard Nine Men's Morris rules, unchanged, redrawn on circular topology: the board has 3 concentric rings of 8 points each (24 total), connected by radial lines at 4 axis points per ring, functionally identical to the traditional square layout. Each player has 9 pieces. Phase 1 (placing): players alternate placing one piece per turn on any empty point; completing a mill (3 of your pieces in a row along a printed line) lets you remove one opponent piece that is not itself in a mill (unless all opponent pieces are in mills). Phase 2 (moving): once all 18 pieces are placed, players alternate sliding one piece along a printed line to an adjacent empty point, still forming/breaking mills to capture; a player reduced to exactly 3 pieces may 'fly' a piece to any empty point instead of a single step. Win by reducing your opponent to 2 pieces or leaving them with no legal move.
ideas.components: 1 board (3 concentric ring tracks with radial connector lines, ~28cm diameter PLA, navy with printed star-field texture, 24 shallow marked points, connector grooves embossed at least 2mm wide for adjacency clarity); 18 pieces (18mm spherical planet-shaped tokens, PLA, 2 colors with a ring/no-ring visual distinction molded in); 1 printed lidded storage box (~30x30x5cm).
ideas.demand_case: Nine Men's Morris is a globally recognized ancient abstract strategy game documented back to the Roman Empire, in continuous modern commercial production (WE Games and NewVenture Games editions currently in retail), giving this reskin an established, rules-literate buyer base. Target audience: casual abstract-strategy buyers and gift shoppers, ages 8+, seeking a striking display-worthy edition of a classic.
ideas.fun_case: Nine Men's Morris's core tension (mill-formation versus blocking, then endgame flying-piece tactics) is a centuries-validated 2-player abstract with real depth in under 20 minutes; this reskin adds no new mechanical fun but targets buyers who choose board games partly as display or gift objects, a segment separate from mechanical-novelty buyers and already served by mancala/chess-reskin sales.
ideas.producibility_notes: Single board plus one token geometry (2 color variants) plus a box; no joints, no assembly, no sub-1mm features. Because the circular redraw is less visually intuitive than the traditional 3-nested-square layout, connector grooves are specified at a minimum 2mm width so ring-vs-radial adjacency is legible at a glance without a rulebook diagram.
